full_text_en:
Nanjing Gulou District Real Estate Management Company, Zhong Baoqiang et al. v. Jiangsu Shengming Industrial Co., Ltd. — dispute over housing infringement

Plaintiff: Nanjing Gulou District Real Estate Management Company, Jiangsu Province. Domicile: No. 24 Yunnan Road, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Legal Representative: He Zhinan, General Manager of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Xu Yan, lawyer of Nanjing Lianhe Law Firm.

Plaintiff: Zhong Baoqiang and 19 other households.
Litigation Representative: Zhong Baoqiang, residing at Room 502, No. 166 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Litigation Representative: Yang Yuanxin, residing at Room 302, No. 164 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Litigation Representative: Cheng Daode, residing at Room 301, No. 166 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Litigation Representative: Xia Xiulan, residing at Room 402, No. 164 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Jiangsu Shengming Industrial Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 166-2 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Legal Representative: Dai Guoliang, General Manager of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Li Weimin, lawyer of Jinling Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Dai Yimin, Deputy Manager of Jiangsu Shengming Industrial Co., Ltd.

The plaintiffs, Nanjing Gulou District Real Estate Management Company (hereinafter referred to as the Real Estate Company) and Zhong Baoqiang and 19 other households, brought an action against the defendant, Jiangsu Shengming Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shengming Company), for dispute over housing infringement to the Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Plaintiff's Allegations

The plaintiffs alleged: The building in which the plaintiffs reside has the ground floor owned by the defendant, while the ownership of the second through sixth floors belongs to the plaintiffs and others. The defendant, without authorization, demolished and renovated the ground floor, dug deep into the indoor ground to install a mezzanine, exposing the foundation beams, and fixed channel steel to the building framework and surrounding walls with expansion bolts, which significantly increased the load on the building's main structure. The defendant's actions caused cracks in the walls of the plaintiffs' residences, water seepage on the roof, and leakage of water pipes, seriously affecting the plaintiffs' safety of residence. The defendant's actions infringed upon the lawful rights and interests of the plaintiffs as property owners. The plaintiffs requested a judgment ordering the defendant to restore the building to its original condition and to take remedial reinforcement measures for the damaged main structure of the building and the water supply and drainage system.

Defendant's Defense

The defendant argued: The defendant carried out decoration and renovation of its own property within its ownership scope. All works were designed by qualified design units, approved by relevant administrative authorities, and recognized by the building safety appraisal authority, thus in no way infringed upon the plaintiffs' rights and interests. The damages claimed by the plaintiffs were quality issues of the building and were unrelated to the defendant's decoration and renovation. The plaintiffs' claims were unfounded and should be dismissed.

Facts Found by the Court at First Instance

The six-story reinforced concrete frame commercial-residential building located at Nos. 164, 166, and 166-2 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, was constructed in 1992. The ground floor, with a floor height of 4.2 meters and a building area of 362.04 square meters, was used for commercial purposes and was owned by the defendant Shengming Company. The second through sixth floors were used as residences. After the reform of the housing system, these floors became owned by the plaintiff Real Estate Company and the plaintiff households including Zhong Baoqiang, respectively.

In March 1998, when the defendant Shengming Company was decorating the ground floor houses in preparation for adding a mezzanine, it removed all the infill walls between the reinforced concrete frame columns and excavated the ground to a depth of 0.9 to 1.2 meters, thereby exposing part of the ground beams, which gave rise to the dispute. In June of the same year, Shengming Company commissioned the Nanjing Building Safety Appraisal Office (hereinafter referred to as the Appraisal Office) to appraise the safety of the proposed mezzanine addition. The conclusion was that the mezzanine construction did not cause apparent structural damage to the main building and did not currently affect the safety of occupancy and use; however, there were issues in the design and construction of the mezzanine, and it was recommended to entrust qualified units for design and construction. Subsequently, Shengming Company carried out rectification as required by the Appraisal Office and, in September of the same year, again commissioned the Appraisal Office to appraise the new design plan for the mezzanine addition. The conclusion was that the formal construction drawings issued by a certified design unit could meet the safety requirements for use, and it was recommended to strengthen supervision during construction to ensure engineering quality. In November of the same year, the Earthquake Resistance Office of the Jiangsu Provincial Construction Committee, after review, approved Shengming Company's mezzanine addition plan; the Fire Prevention Section of the Gulou District Public Security Sub-bureau of Nanjing, after review, approved Shengming Company to construct according to the submitted drawings. The plaintiff Real Estate Company and the plaintiff households including Zhong Baoqiang disagreed with Shengming Company's construction according to the design plan and filed the lawsuit in January 1999.

During the trial, the defendant Shengming Company obtained a Construction Project Planning Permit issued by the Nanjing Municipal Planning Bureau, authorizing the addition of a mezzanine indoors at No. 166-2 Louzi Alley, Nanjing. The court commissioned the Appraisal Office to appraise the housing damage claimed by the plaintiff households including Zhong Baoqiang. The conclusion was that the building was in a basically sound condition. The issues of cracks in wall tiles, panels, and internal corners in the houses of Zhong Baoqiang and other households were not caused by Shengming Company's mezzanine addition. It was recommended that Shengming Company plaster the wall cracks in the staircase of the large platform common area on the ground floor with high-grade cement mortar and apply a protective layer to the exposed parts of the ground beams.

The above facts are confirmed by the following evidence: ownership certificates, construction drawings for the indoor mezzanine renovation at No. 166-2 Louzi Alley, appraisal reports, seismic review form for building mezzanine renovation works, review opinion on building design fire prevention, construction project planning permit, payment receipts, and other evidence.

Opinion of the Court at First Instance

The court at first instance held: Article 83 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The neighboring parties in immovable property shall correctly handle such neighboring relations as water interception, drainage, passage, ventilation, and lighting in the spirit of being conducive to production, convenient living, unity and mutual assistance, as well as fair and reasonable. If a neighboring party causes obstruction or loss to the other, it shall cease the infringement, remove the obstruction, and compensate for the loss." The plaintiff Real Estate Company and the households of Zhong Baoqiang et al., and the defendant Shengming Company are neighboring parties in immovable property. They should properly handle neighboring relations in accordance with the law and jointly maintain the safety of the building in which they reside. When Shengming Company added a mezzanine within its own ownership scope, the new plan was designed by a qualified design department and approved by the administrative authorities for construction planning, earthquake resistance, and fire protection. If Shengming Company could organize the construction with strict supervision in accordance with the approved construction quality standards, the safety of the building could be ensured. The Real Estate Company and Zhong Baoqiang et al. claimed that the damage to the houses on the second through sixth floors was caused by Shengming Company's mezzanine addition; Shengming Company had provided evidence that it was not related, and the Real Estate Company and Zhong Baoqiang et al. did not adduce rebuttal evidence. The court did not support the claims of the Real Estate Company and Zhong Baoqiang et al. based on this ground. Since the construction caused interference to the neighboring parties, Shengming Company voluntarily offered to compensate each household of Zhong Baoqiang et al. with RMB 1,000, which should be permitted. Accordingly, the court rendered the following judgment:

1. The defendant Shengming Company shall plaster the wall cracks in the staircase of the large platform common area on the ground floor of the building with high-grade cement mortar, apply a protective layer to the exposed parts of the ground beams, and dredge the downpipes. The plaintiff Real Estate Company and Shengming Company shall jointly commission a supervision department to be responsible for on-site supervision, with supervision costs borne by Shengming Company.

2. The defendant Shengming Company shall pay RMB 1,000 in compensation to each household of the plaintiff Zhong Baoqiang et al.

The plaintiff households of Zhong Baoqiang et al., dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Nanjing Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province on the same grounds as in their initial complaint, requesting the reversal of the original judgment and a new judgment in their favor.

Facts Found by the Court of Second Instance

The Nanjing Intermediate People's Court, upon trial, held:

The facts found in the first instance were basically correct and fully supported by evidence.

The appellant households of Zhong Baoqiang et al. and the original plaintiff Real Estate Company, by virtue of their ownership rights in the immovable property, formed neighboring relations in immovable property with the appellee Shengming Company. The right of neighboring relations in immovable property is a limitation and extension of immovable property ownership, being a property right related to immovable property ownership. Without immovable property ownership, there can be no neighboring rights in immovable property. Therefore, to properly resolve disputes over neighboring relations in immovable property, it is essential to correctly grasp the forms of immovable property ownership of the neighboring parties.

In the past, the form of housing ownership in China was that a single independent building was owned by one person (i.e., one thing, one right). With the reform of the housing system, the phenomenon of a single independent building being owned by multiple persons (i.e., one thing, multiple rights) has become increasingly common.

For a single independent building constructed by a building investment entity, it must have foundations, frames, load-bearing walls, partitions, roofs, corridors, stairs, doors, windows, various pipelines, and necessary activity spaces to allow the differentiation of specific spaces for independent use by different persons. These two parts must be combined for the building to exist independently. Only when the building exists independently can the specific spaces for independent use by different persons perform their functions. When a single independent building possesses the physical conditions for differentiating specific spaces for independent use, and the building investment entity transfers these spaces respectively to different purchasers, resulting in the building being owned by multiple persons, the architectural characteristics of the building determine that each owner acquires partitioned ownership rights in the building. This is a right not entirely identical to the ownership in the form of one thing, one right. In a contract for the transfer of partitioned ownership of a building, although it only specifies the transfer of spaces that can be differentiated for independent use (hereinafter referred to as exclusive portions), this does not mean that the foundations, frames, load-bearing walls, partitions, roofs, corridors, stairs, doors, windows, various pipelines, and necessary activity spaces (hereinafter referred to as common portions) are not transferred. If there were no transfer of common portions, the exclusive portions would not become objects of the property right of ownership that could be transferred. It is only because the common portions are necessarily transferred together with the exclusive portions that there is no need to register each common portion transferred with the transfer in the contract.

Partitioned ownership of a building first refers to the right of all partitioned owners to the entirety of the independent building and all common facilities within the building, and secondly refers to the exclusive right of each partitioned owner to a specific space. The common ownership right in partitioned ownership of a building is indivisible and can only be transferred together with the exclusive right. The right holder is entitled to legitimately use the common portions according to their type, nature, structure, and purpose; to share in the proceeds arising from the whole building or the common portions of the building; and to prevent any infringement upon the whole building or the common portions of the building. While enjoying rights, the right holder must fulfill the following obligations: maintain the status quo of the common portions and not demand partition; maintain the normal use condition of the common portions and not encroach upon, alter, or damage them; and bear reasonably apportioned expenses necessary for maintaining the normal use of the common portions. Under this form of right, since the entire building and all common facilities within it are owned in common by all partitioned owners, all partitioned owners need to enjoy rights and bear obligations with respect to the entire building, and they may form a group legal relationship in this regard; since specific parts of the building are exclusively owned by each partitioned owner, each partitioned owner needs to exercise rights and bear obligations with respect to their exclusive portion, thereby forming a zonal ownership legal relationship with others; and since each partitioned owner enjoys rights equivalent to ownership of an independent building with respect to a specific space, each partitioned owner forms neighboring legal relations with other owners of adjacent immovable property.

The six-story commercial-residential building located at Nos. 164, 166, and 166-2 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, is partitioned among the appellant households of Zhong Baoqiang et al., the original plaintiff Real Estate Company, and the appellee Shengming Company. Each partitioned owner possesses both independent ownership of their respective exclusive portions and common ownership of the entire building and its common portions. Exclusive portions refer to building spaces enclosed above, below, and on all sides by building materials. Apart from these, the other parts of the building (including the buried works below the ground floor floor) shall be deemed common portions. Any alteration to common portions must not be contrary to the common interest and requires the consent of all partitioned owners; otherwise, it constitutes an infringement upon the common ownership rights of other right holders.

Although the appellee Shengming Company added the mezzanine within its exclusive portion, its action of adding the mezzanine made use of the beams, columns, and buried works below the floor, which belong to the common portions, thereby increasing the load on the beams and columns and exposing the ground beams. This constitutes an abnormal use of the common portions, affecting the common interests of all partitioned owners. Although Shengming Company's action of adding the mezzanine was approved by the administrative authorities, this only means that from the perspective of administrative management, the administrative authorities do not consider the action to be capable of causing harm to society and thus may be implemented. Since adding the mezzanine required the use of common portions of the building, and the ownership of the common portions of the building is held by all partitioned owners, not by the approving administrative authority, whether the action of adding the mezzanine should be implemented must be decided by Shengming Company after soliciting the opinions of all partitioned owners. Shengming Company's argument that it was carrying out decoration and renovation of its own property within its ownership scope cannot be sustained. Regardless of whether the houses of the appellant households of Zhong Baoqiang et al. were damaged, and regardless of whether such damage was related to Shengming Company, Shengming Company's addition of a mezzanine for itself by using the common portions without obtaining the consent of all partitioned owners constitutes an infringement upon the common ownership rights of the other partitioned owners. Therefore, the appeal lodged by Zhong Baoqiang et al. on the ground that Shengming Company infringed upon the lawful rights and interests of the property owners should be upheld. Shengming Company shall dismantle the mezzanine and restore the excavated parts to their original condition. The original judgment, in resolving the dispute by applying the legal provisions on neighboring relations without analyzing the form of housing ownership of each party, applied the law incorrectly. The original judgment ordering Shengming Company to plaster the wall cracks in the staircase of the large platform common area on the ground floor with high-grade cement mortar, to apply a protective layer to the exposed parts of the ground beams, and to dredge the downpipes was correct; however, it was erroneous to deny the claims of the Real Estate Company and Zhong Baoqiang et al. on the ground that the damage to their houses was unrelated to Shengming Company, and this part should be reversed. Accordingly, the Nanjing Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Items (1) and (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on July 21, 2000:

1. Affirm Item 1 of the judgment of first instance;
2. Reverse Item 2 of the judgment of first instance;
3. The appellee Shengming Company shall, within sixty days from the effective date of this judgment, dismantle the mezzanine in the ground floor house at No. 166-2 Louzi Alley, Nanjing, and restore the excavated parts to their original condition. The original plaintiff Real Estate Company, the appellant households of Zhong Baoqiang et al., and Shengming Company shall jointly commission a supervision department to be responsible for on-site supervision of the construction, with supervision costs borne by Shengming Company.

The costs of the first instance (RMB 150), the costs of the second instance (RMB 150), and the appraisal fees (RMB 6,208), totaling RMB 6,508, shall be borne by the appellee Shengming Company.
